links.comparator_used: Direct ophthalmologist review of all fundus photographs / standard human interpretation without AI-negative cases being automatically classified as negative
links.outcome: Ophthalmologist review workload and diagnostic sensitivity/specificity for DR, RVO, AMD
links.effect: Review reduced to 7.3%-8.0% of images for DR, 11.7%-11.9% for RVO, and 13.5%-16.8% for AMD. DR sensitivity decreased from 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference, -0.0330; 95% CI, -0.0495 to -0.0165; p < 0.001) with specificity not significantly changed (0.9961 to 0.9983; p = 0.183). RVO sensitivity was unchanged (0.9807) and specificity did not change significantly (0.9985 to 0.9988; p = 0.320). AMD sensitivity decreased from 0.8570 to 0.8445 (difference, -0.0124; 95% CI, -0.0215 to -0.0033; p = 0.008), with specificity not significantly changed (0.9685 to 0.9843; p = 0.324).
links.tradeoff: Reduced ophthalmologist workload, but reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD, meaning some true-positive cases would go undetected and diagnosis/treatment could be delayed.
links.quote: AI-assisted negative-screening can reduce ophthalmologist workload across multiple retinal diseases, but with disease-specific safety trade-offs: because AI-negative images are not reviewed, reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD means a small proportion of true-positive cases would go undetected, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment for sight-threatening disease.
